What lies below is for Hild and Corm to go down to, at Brun's side. Quest effectively resolved; the sixty are to be brought up for burial.

entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

You touch Corm's shoulder and the spell's pale warmth settles over him like a cloak. The old dwarf's shoulders ease. You open Father Dorrin's book to the captain's rite, lay your holy symbol against the iron beside the heartstone, and begin.

The Morninglord's invocation comes first, plain and unhurried. Then the names. You say them as if they were your own family's, one at a time, each a breath long, and the cold in the gallery seems to lean closer with every one. Hild's lips move silently with them. Garrick, at the bend, takes off his hood.

Your voice does not falter. When you come to the last, you let the silence gather a moment, and then you say, "Brenn Ironvein," and Hild makes a small sound in her throat.

The heartstone does not flare or crack. It simply grows warm, then warmer, the way a hearth does when someone feeds it, and the faint lines of the seal on the door's face brighten once, gold as morning, and go out like a lit lamp set down. A long breath runs through the stone. It is not a roar. It sounds like a very old, very tired thing letting go of something it has held too long.

Then the iron bands loosen, and the door stands unbarred.

No horror comes through. Cool, clean air moves up from the dark, smelling of wet stone and, faintly, thyme. Corm does not take his hand away. His face is wet and he is smiling, the first time you have seen it. Somewhere far below, so faint you might have dreamed it, a voice says a word in Dwarvish that might have been *thank you*, or only the wind.

Hild steps forward, and her hand finds Corm's, and she says to you hoarsely, "Come down with us, Stonehearth. I'd not meet him alone."

The rite is done, and the first of your promises is kept. You also earned 200 XP, which brings you to 900, enough for level 3. Your spells are mostly ready, with two slots left, and Channel Divinity untouched.

Shall we take your third level now, or go down first? What does Brun do?

sheet.name: Brunhilde Stonehearth
sheet.opening: Brunhilde "Brun" Stonehearth, a stocky Hill Dwarf cleric of the Morninglord (Life domain), auburn braid threaded with brass beads, dented but polished chain mail, warhammer worn smooth at the grip, carries the prayer book of her late foster-father figure, Father Dorrin Ashbeard, the old priest who found her as a half-starved orphan in a collapsed mine shaft outside a hill-hold and raised her in his small shrine. She is optimistic, tries to find common ground even between fierce enemies, is suspicious of strangers, and wants to repay the mercy she was shown by walking into danger to keep others alive (ideal: Charity). Opening: it is late afternoon and Brun has just arrived at a rain-soaked crossroads waystation on a mountain road, a squat stone inn and shrine-lean-to shared by travelers, having come down from the hills to carry Father Dorrin's blessing to those in need. A fresh rockslide has just buried part of the road beyond the station, and muffled tapping and a faint cry for help are coming from beneath the stones: a wagon of travelers (a wounded merchant, a child, and a mule-driver) is trapped, and a group of wary, mismatched strangers (a nervous caravan guard, a sullen hunter, and the innkeeper) is arguing over whether it is safe to dig or whether the whole slope will come down. The hurt need a healer now, and the strangers need someone to pull them together before the mountain moves again. Brun, who knows exactly what it is to be trapped under stone and found, is the one they turn to. Her Stonecunning and Smith's Tools may help read the unstable rock and shore it up; her spells (Healing Word, Cure Wounds, Bless, Sanctuary) may keep people alive. The sixty were found at rest, Brenn holding the sleeper's 'hand' (a hollow of warm stone). Hild and Corm will carry the dead up for burial. Corm freed from keeping.

entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

Your hand on Corm's shoulder lends him the spell's ward, a faint gold sheen along the scarred arm, and you begin. The Morninglord's invocation first, then the names, one after another, steady as beads on a cord. The tunnel is silent but for your voice. Somewhere around the thirtieth name you feel the iron under your holy symbol warm. At the fiftieth, the heartstone begins to glow like a coal. Hild's lips move with every name she knows.

You reach the last. "Brenn Ironvein." Hild makes a sound like a breaking branch.

Silence. Then the stone lets out a long, low sigh, not a roar, the sound of a very old thing setting down a weight. The hum drains out of your teeth. The bands of the door loosen one by one, and it swings inward on its own, without a squeal, onto a gallery lit faintly gold.

There is no horror. The sixty lie where they chose to lie, peaceful in the dry cold, long past harm. At the far end, beside a hollow of warm stone shaped like a great cupped hand, a dwarf with Hild's jaw sits with his own hand resting in it, his eyes closed, as if he had only just fallen asleep. The warmth fades from the stone as you watch, and goes out like a candle, with a feeling of gratitude.

Hild crosses the gallery on her knees. Corm lowers his arm, the scar no longer bright, and weeps without a sound. Garrick takes off his hood.

The seal is mended in the only way it could be, and you have 900 XP, enough for level 3. The Hearthdeep dead will need carrying up and burying, and Pip is owed her bell and her story.

You can level up now. Would you like to do that first?

entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

Warmth in your palm, a murmur of the Morninglord's light, and Corm's shoulders ease under the ward as you lay your hand against his arm. Then you begin.

The invocation comes steady. The first names fall one by one into the cold, and the door seems to listen. Twenty names, thirty. Hild's lips move with each. Then, near the fortieth, you reach for a name and find two crowding the same place in your mouth, a father's and a son's, and you say the wrong one first. You catch it and go back, but the cadence is broken, and the stone feels it.

The door shudders. A deep sound rolls out of the rock, not a roar but something like a held breath let go, and the iron bands ring. Dust sifts from the timbers. Behind the door the sleeper is awake. You feel it rather than hear it: a vast, aching grief pressing on your chest, old as the hill, and under it a tremor of fear that the voice speaking its dead has faltered.

Corm's hand does not leave the stone, though his knees buckle. The ward holds him steady. Hild has gone grey and Garrick's hand is on his bow at the bend, unstrung, useless. The heartstone glows a dull amber, flickering.

The rite is not lost. Twenty names remain, and Brenn's last, but the sleeper is listening now and it is afraid. You have two first-level slots, Channel Divinity, and your voice. What does Brun do?

entries.text: notebook: updated Mend the Hearthdeep Seal

Your hand rests on the cold iron, your holy symbol beside the heartstone, and the protective warmth of the spell settles over Corm like a cloak. You begin.

The Morninglord's invocation comes first, and the old Dwarvish rolls out clean and steady in the tunnel. Then the names, one at a time, each one set down like a stone in a cairn. The words do not stumble, because you have carried them all night. Somewhere past the thirtieth the heartstone begins to glow, a soft gold like the first edge of sunrise. At the fortieth the hum returns, deep in your breastbone, and it does not feel like a threat. It sounds like someone listening.

Corm's arm trembles, but his palm stays pressed to the stone. Hild's lips move with every name, and when you reach the fifty-ninth she is weeping openly. You draw breath and say the last: "Brenn Ironvein."

The door sighs. Iron bands loosen and fall away in flakes of rust, and the stone swings inward on hinges that have not moved in forty winters. There is no roar and no rage. A long, slow breath rolls out of the dark, cool and clean, smelling of wet earth and rain on rock, and the gold light flows past you and down into the deep. For a moment you feel something vast and old brush your shoulder, the way a tired child leans against a parent. Then it is gone, up through the hill and out into the morning.

Beyond the door lies the gallery. The sixty are there, resting where they sat down, bones in the old miners' cloaks, peaceful. At the far end one dwarf sits against the wall with his hand curled around a smooth, round stone, as if holding someone else's fingers. Hild goes to him on her knees.

Corm lifts his hand from the heartstone, the scar on his forearm pale and quiet, his burden gone. "It's finished," he says. "Gods, it's finished." Behind you Garrick lets his breath out and nods once.

You have earned 200 XP for ending the seal with mercy, bringing you to 900 XP, and you can now rise to level 3. First-level slots: you have 2 of 3 left, and Channel Divinity is unspent.

Brun falls into step beside Maren and shortens her stride to match. "Aunt Maren, while we walk, would you tell me about the Deepwatch itself, and about my mother as a girl? I'd like to hear the small things, like what she liked to eat and what songs she sang."

input.add_to_description: Day 5 road talk (Maren's memories): as a girl Sigrun chalked maps on every flat stone, loved honey-oat cakes and pickled mushrooms, sang the miners' tally-song 'Seven Lamps' off-key and cheerfully, and once tied a rope to a goat to measure a cliff. She hated being told a shaft was unsafe. Maren says Brun hums the same tune when she works.

Maren's description: a hall cut into the face of a mountain above a green tarn, with a lantern kept lit in its high window every night for those still below ground. Its Long Gallery holds the names of every lost miner carved in rows. About a day and a half from the waymark-hut.

entries.text:
Maren's pace slows further when you ask, as if the words need room, and she tells you for the better part of five hours.

The Deepwatch, she says, is a hall cut into the face of a mountain above a green tarn, with a single lantern kept lit in its highest window every night for those still underground. In its Long Gallery every lost miner's name is carved in rows, and the stonecutters add new ones each winter. Children of the wardens learn to read there by tracing the letters with a finger.

And your mother, small and stubborn, chalking maps on every flat stone she could find until the cooks begged the elders to give her slate. She loved honey-oat cakes and pickled mushrooms, which no one else would touch, and she sang the miners' tally-song, "Seven Lamps," badly and cheerfully at the top of her lungs. Once she tied a rope to a goat to measure a cliff. The goat survived. "You hum it," Maren says, not looking at you. "That tune. You have been humming it for an hour and don't know."

You realize you have. Garrick, ahead, very carefully does not turn round.

You are still a little unsure what to make of the thing you found tucked in the binding of Father Dorrin's prayer book, two folded letters in his small hand, addressed to the Deepwatch and never sent. Maren looked at them once, her lips pressed thin, and said only, "Read them where it is quiet."

Near seven-thirty the waymark-hut comes into view on its saddle: a squat circle of dry-stone with a turf roof, a hearth, and a warden's sign over the lintel. The wind is rising, the sky going the color of old pewter. Garrick has already scouted it and signals all clear.

You promised to cook. You have two rations, the innkeeper's wife's oatcakes and dried apple, and a little salt from the pack. Garrick has ten rations of his own and a mess kit.

What does Brun do?

Brun falls into step beside Maren and shortens her stride to match. "Aunt Maren, while we walk, would you tell me about the Deepwatch itself, and about my mother as a girl? I'd like to hear the small things, like what she liked to eat and what songs she sang."

input.add_to_description: Told by Maren on the road: as a girl Sigrun sang the miners' work-song 'Seven Lamps' off-key on purpose, loved honeyed barley cakes and hated mutton fat, and once mapped the Deepwatch cellars at age nine and was caught in a drain. Maren also says Sigrun kept a secret she never told the Deepwatch about Brun's father.

Per Maren: a hall cut into a cliff face above a glacial tarn, seven lamps burning in its high windows, one for each founding warden-house; gates of black oak banded in iron; archives in the lower vaults. The wardens there are few now, perhaps forty. Father Dorrin's two sealed letters are addressed to its Lampkeeper.

entries.text: time: 3 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 5:59 PM

Maren is quiet for a few steps, as if sorting a drawer of old things, and then she begins.

The Deepwatch, she says, is cut into a cliff face above a glacial tarn, with seven lamps in its high windows, one for each of the founding warden-houses, and they have not gone dark in four hundred years. Gates of black oak banded in iron. The archives lie in the lower vaults, cold and dry, and a good half of the old holds' names are written there. There are perhaps forty wardens left, she says, and fewer every winter.

Then she tells you about Sigrun. As a girl she sang the miners' work-song "Seven Lamps" badly on purpose, to annoy the choirmaster. She loved honeyed barley cakes and loathed mutton fat, and at nine she mapped the whole of the Deepwatch cellars and got stuck in a drain doing it, and had to be fished out by her ankles. "She was a terror," Maren says, and laughs, a dry little cough of a laugh. "You have her chin and her temper. I see both."

Once, a little later, her voice drops. "She kept one thing from us, your mother. About your father. She said she would tell when she was ready. She was not given the time."

You walk on a while in the long light. Garrick finds a game trail along the ridge. At the waymark-hut, a squat stone shelter at the saddle with a turf roof and a rusted iron lamp-hook over the door, you find dry wood stacked and the old warden's sign scratched by the lintel. You cook, as you promised: oatcakes crisped on the hearthstone, and a stew of dried apple, onion and the last of the salt pork, with a pinch of the thyme pressed in Father Dorrin's book. Garrick eats three bowls and says it is the best he's had in a decade. It is nearly six.

Unpacking the prayer book to read the evening prayers, you feel something tucked inside the back binding that you had not noticed before: two folded letters, sealed in grey wax with the sun of the Morninglord, and addressed in Father Dorrin's cramped hand to *The Lampkeeper of the Deepwatch*. Maren sees them and goes very still. "That is his hand," she whispers. "Those were never delivered."

You are at full strength with three spell slots, in a warm hut with kin and a friend. The seals are unbroken.

entries.text: time: 3 hours 30 minutes later: Day 5, 5:59 PM

Maren is quiet for a few strides, and then she begins, and once she has begun she does not stop.

Your mother, she says, loved honey-oat cakes and burnt the first batch every single time, and ate them anyway, scowling. She sang the old shaft-song, "Lamp Before Me," off-key and at the top of her voice while she worked, so that a whole gallery could find her by ear. She kept a ledger of every lamp she ever lit, down to the oil, and teased the others for losing count of theirs. She was afraid of heights but never of depth. "She'd go down into any dark you pointed her at," Maren says, "and come up complaining about the lunch."

You laugh before you realise you are going to, and it catches in your throat.

Of the Deepwatch she tells you more. It is cut into a cliff-face above a cold grey lake, a stair of lamp-lit terraces climbing the rock, with the Hall of Names at the heart of it, where every warden's record is kept and the lamps are never allowed to go out. There are few wardens left, she admits, but kin come home each midwinter, and the lamps are always trimmed for them.

She asks, mildly, about the thing tucked in the back of Father Dorrin's book. You had found it only that morning as you packed: two letters, folded small and sealed in old wax, both addressed in his cramped hand to the Deepwatch. Maren looks at them a long time without touching them. "He did write more than once," she says. "I think they never reached us. Keep them dry. We will read them in the Hall."

By evening the sun is low and red on the hills, and you reach the saddle. The waymark-hut sits on it like a thumb of grey stone, roofed with turf, with a hearth, a woodpile, and a stack of bunks. You cook, as you promised: oatcakes browned on the hearthstone, a stew of dried mutton and apple, and, in your mother's honor, a deliberately burnt first batch that makes Maren laugh until she coughs. Garrick eats three bowls and says it is the best food he has had since his mother's.

Your voice carries over the wind. For a breath the sentry is silent, and the rain drums on his hood. Then he cries out, a short, cracked sound, and is gone from the parapet. A bell begins to ring somewhere inside the mountain, slow and deep, and then another answers it from higher up.

He steps aside and lifts one hand toward the warm hall beyond.

"The Hall of Names is lit," he says, more quietly. "It has been lit every night since the day she died. Whenever you are ready, Sigrun's daughter, there is a page I would like you to read. But there is soup first, and dry clothes, and no one in this mountain will think the less of you for either."

line:
Brun squares her shoulders, wipes the rain from her face, and calls up to the sentry in clear Dwarvish, "I'm Brunhilde Stonehearth, Sigrun's daughter, raised by Father Dorrin Ashbeard. I carry a copy of the Hearthdeep warden-captain's ledger, and I've come home."

She keeps one hand on Maren's arm and glances at Garrick. "Stay close, friend. You're with me, and you're welcome here."

input.description: Stern captain of the Deepwatch wardens, Maren's rival of forty years and, she admits, her only friend. Disapproved of Sigrun's marriage to a lamp-maker who would not swear the oath. Meets Brun at the gate on Day 6 evening.

input.add_to_description: Day 6 evening: Brun announced herself at the gate with the ledger copy. The doors opened and Captain Torvald Greycairn came out. Two sealed letters in Father Dorrin's hand, addressed to the Deepwatch, were found tucked behind the prayer book's back cover; unread, still sealed.

entries.text:
Your voice goes up the wet cliff clear and level, and for a moment the only answer is the storm. Then the sentry's lantern swings away, and a horn sounds somewhere inside the mountain, one long note and two short.

The bronze doors open inward a handspan at a time, with a grinding that you feel in your boots. Lamplight pours out across the wet stone. Wardens in grey cloaks line the passage, a dozen of them, hammer-and-three-lines brooches at every shoulder, and not one speaks.

Then a broad, grey-bearded dwarf walks out through the doors with no cloak against the rain, a heavy iron-headed staff in one hand, and stops three paces from you. His face is carved from the same stone as the gate. He looks at your chin, your braid, the dented mail. His eyes stop on the iron ring.

"Torvald Greycairn," Maren says at your side, dry as ever. "Captain of the Deepwatch. Try not to be disagreeable, Torvald."

He does not answer her. He says to you, in a voice like a door on a rusted hinge, "You have her chin." A long breath. "The ledger. Show it."

You reach into your pack to unwrap Corm's gift, and your fingers close on something you did not put there: two letters, sealed in grey wax, tucked behind the back cover of Father Dorrin's prayer book. They are in his cramped hand, addressed to the Deepwatch, and the seals are unbroken. He must have hidden them years ago, for you to find only now.

Torvald sees them. His jaw tightens, and the rain runs down his beard.

Behind him the lamps of the seven galleries burn in the dark. Garrick has gone very still at your shoulder. Maren's hand tightens on your arm.

What does Brun do?

sheet.opening: Brunhilde "Brun" Stonehearth, a stocky Hill Dwarf cleric of the Morninglord (Life domain), auburn braid threaded with brass beads, dented but polished chain mail, warhammer worn smooth at the grip, carries the prayer book of her late foster-father figure, Father Dorrin Ashbeard, the old priest who found her as a half-starved orphan in a collapsed mine shaft outside a hill-hold and raised her in his small shrine. She is optimistic, tries to find common ground even between fierce enemies, is suspicious of strangers, and wants to repay the mercy she was shown by walking into danger to keep others alive (ideal: Charity). Opening: it is late afternoon and Brun has just arrived at a rain-soaked crossroads waystation on a mountain road, a squat stone inn and shrine-lean-to shared by travelers, having come down from the hills to carry Father Dorrin's blessing to those in need. A fresh rockslide has just buried part of the road beyond the station, and muffled tapping and a faint cry for help are coming from beneath the stones: a wagon of travelers (a wounded merchant, a child, and a mule-driver) is trapped, and a group of wary, mismatched strangers (a nervous caravan guard, a sullen hunter, and the innkeeper) is arguing over whether it is safe to dig or whether the whole slope will come down. The hurt need a healer now, and the strangers need someone to pull them together before the mountain moves again. Brun, who knows exactly what it is to be trapped under stone and found, is the one they turn to. Her Stonecunning and Smith's Tools may help read the unstable rock and shore it up; her spells (Healing Word, Cure Wounds, Bless, Sanctuary) may keep people alive. Keep the backstory true: Father Dorrin raised her long ago and she carries his book; nothing about it is recent or lost.
